paraphrase: Dignāga salutes the Buddha, who has become a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-bhūta), seeks the welfare of the world, is the teacher, the Sugata and the protector, and resolves to compile, for the establishment of valid cognition, a compendium of his own scattered views.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: There are only two means of valid cognition, perception and inference, because the object to be known has two characteristics — its own particular character and the general character; there is no further object, so there is no further means.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: Perception is free of conceptual construction; construction is the joining of a name, a genus and the like (to what is perceived).
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: Mental perception includes the awareness of an object and the self-awareness of desire and other feelings, which is free of construction; so is the yogins' vision of the object alone, unmixed with the teacher's instruction. Erroneous cognition, conventional cognition, inference and memory are pseudo-perceptions.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: The means of knowledge is the cognition itself as having the form of the object, and its result is that same cognition as self-awareness; a cognition arises with two appearances, of itself and of the object, and its self-awareness is the result — so the distinction of means, object and result is only figurative, for cognition is one.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: Inference for oneself is seeing the object through a reason having three characteristics; the reliable word (āptavāda) is a form of inference, because it is like inference in not deceiving.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: Inference for others is making known to another the object one has seen oneself, by stating the triple-marked reason; a thesis is what one intends to prove oneself, not contradicted by perception, inference, one's own doctrine or common usage.
notes: Sanskrit lost (reconstructed ch. 1); paraphrase from memory of the verse and its standard citations; to be checked.

paraphrase: A word does not denote the particulars, which are infinite, nor a real universal; it expresses its object through the exclusion of other objects (anyāpoha) — as 'tree' denotes by excluding the non-tree.
